OP

The fundamental LINK thesis is slightly stronger, primarily because CCIP continues spreading into actual asset movement rather than simply accumulating partnership announcements.

General Tensor bringing TAO to Base is a good example of what I want to see: an asset actually using CCIP to become usable somewhere it previously wasn't.

At this point, however, I would rank the four signals we're tracking like this:

1. CCIP competitive migrations — strongest signal
2. Chainlink Reserve accumulation — strongest LINK-specific signal
3. Institutional/RWA integrations — increasingly strong
4. Transparent revenue/fee growth — still the missing piece

In other words, chainlink might be being used, but it's not translating into fees and revenue. We need to see this change before we can hope for meaningful price appreciation from here.

What do you think? Is it time to bet the farm on link, or has the ship sailed?

Considering its 3 billion budget, GTA 6 may really struggle to do well financially, regardless of its quality - it will…

Open thread • Replies: 19 • Updated: 2026-09-02 12:46 UTC

OP

Considering its 3 billion budget, GTA 6 may really struggle to do well financially, regardless of its quality - it will definitely make a profit in the long run - but that's the point - investors expect quick return - not to wait another 10 years on top of its 10-year development period:

Apparently there are only 100 million consoles capable of running it - so, let's say 50% of that times 80 dollars is "only" 4 billion.
Another sources of income - GTA 6 Online won't be available on release - will take another year or two, PC version is irrelevant - in this economy people can't afford a computer capable of running it, so sale numbers will be marginal (relatively - would be more than great for any other game).

To get the return they expect (at least 10 billion) will take them a long time and may not be free - development and maintenance of Online and PC version may cost them another billion.

Honestly, GTA 6 may kill the game industry even despite being (critically and in terms of sale numbers) a massive success - cost of development getting too high to justify contrasted with what customers are able (not just willing, but financially capable as the whole base) to give in return - games may have simply gotten too big for this world.
